title: Top K Frequent Elements
prompt:
Students searched the library catalog. Given the list of searched book ids, return the k most frequent ids. You may return them in any order (the tests sort your answer). The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

Write topKFrequent(nums, k). A finished MinHeap class is at the top of the editor.

  • topKFrequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2) returns [1, 2]
  • topKFrequent([4], 1) returns [4]
  • topKFrequent([5, -1, -1, 5, 7, -1], 1) returns [-1]

Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 105; 1 <= k <= number of distinct values. Target: better than O(n log n): O(n log k).

tests.name: k equals the number of distinct values
returns values, not counts
tests.code: assertEqual(topKFrequent([10, 10, 20, 20, 20, 30], 1), [20], 'return the value 20, not its count 3');

hints: Trigger: "k most frequent" = two patterns stacked: a frequency map (hashing) to count, then a top-k heap on the counts.
Count into a Map. Then walk the map's entries and push [count, value] into a min-heap compared by count, popping whenever it holds more than k. The survivors are the k most frequent.

Shape:

const heap = new MinHeap((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
for (const [value, count] of counts) {
  heap.push([count, value]);
  if (heap.size() > k) heap.pop();
}
explain:
Time O(n + d log k) where d is the number of distinct values (d is at most n, so O(n log k) overall). Space O(d + k) for the map and heap. Sorting the d entries by count (O(d log d)) is the simpler answer and fine to say first. There is also an O(n) "bucket sort" trick: make an array indexed by count (counts can't exceed n) and read it from the top.

Say it: "Count with a hash map, then keep a size-k min-heap keyed on count. O(n log k). If k is near d I'd just sort the entries; if I need O(n), buckets by frequency."
